findings.name: billing
findings.root_cause: Pod billing-597d6775c9-ht8g5 is stuck Pending with CreateContainerConfigError because its container uses envFrom referencing configmap "billing-config", which does not exist in the billing namespace (only kube-root-ca.crt exists).
findings.fix: Create the missing ConfigMap billing-config in namespace billing with the keys the app expects, or remove the envFrom reference from the Deployment if it is no longer needed.

diagnosis.summary: billing deployment's single pod is stuck Pending with CreateContainerConfigError: the container's envFrom references configmap \"billing-config\" which does not exist in the billing namespace. Creating that ConfigMap (or removing the envFrom reference) will let the pod start.

findings.name: mailer
findings.root_cause: mailer crash-loops with 'nc: bad address smtp-relay' because its pod has dnsPolicy None and a custom dnsConfig pointing nameservers at 10.96.0.99, which does not resolve the cluster's service DNS, so the Service name smtp-relay cannot be resolved even though the relay is up.
findings.fix: Remove the custom dnsConfig (or set dnsPolicy to ClusterFirst) on the mailer Deployment so it uses the cluster DNS resolver; the relay itself is healthy and needs no change.

diagnosis.summary: The relay is NOT down: smtp-relay Service has 1 ready endpoint and its pod is running. The mailer fails because its pod overrides DNS (dnsPolicy None, nameserver 10.96.0.99), so 'smtp-relay' fails to resolve ('bad address') and the container exits 1 in a restart loop. Fix is on the mailer Deployment's DNS config, not the relay.

findings.name: orders-api
findings.root_cause: orders-api container exits 1 on startup with "FATAL: DATABASE_URL is not set" because the Deployment defines no env/envFrom for it; the pod crash-loops (5 restarts, BackOff) and never becomes ready, so the orders page is down.
findings.fix: Add the missing configuration to the orders-api Deployment: set DATABASE_URL via an env var sourced from a Secret/ConfigMap (or add an envFrom referencing the config that holds it), then roll out.

diagnosis.summary: orders/orders-api is crash-looping (exit code 1, 5 restarts, BackOff). Its log shows the app starts, loads config from environment, then dies with 'FATAL: DATABASE_URL is not set'. The pod spec confirms the container has no env or envFrom entries, so the required database URL is simply not configured. This single root cause explains both the restarts and the down orders page. Fix: add DATABASE_URL (from a Secret/ConfigMap) to the orders-api Deployment.

findings.name: stock-db
findings.root_cause: stock-db's memory limit of 24Mi is far too small for its workload (it loads a stock index into memory), so the kernel OOMKills it (exit 137) in a restart loop; with no ready replica, port 5432 is down and stock-api crashes with 'stock-db:5432 unreachable'.
findings.fix: Raise stock-db's memory request/limit well above 24Mi (e.g. 256Mi or more based on the actual stock-index size) so it survives the index load and stays up.

diagnosis.summary: stock-api's crash loop is a symptom, not the cause. Its logs show 'stock-db:5432 unreachable' because the stock-db Deployment is stuck in an OOMKill/restart loop: its container has a 24Mi memory limit/request, but after ~25s it loads a stock index into memory and gets OOMKilled (exit 137, 3 restarts, BackOff events). No stock-db pod is ever ready, so nothing listens on 5432 and stock-api exits with code 1. Fix: increase stock-db's memory limit.

findings.name: frontend

findings.fix: Change the Deployment's container image to a tag that exists (e.g. nginx:1.27-alpine or the intended published tag) and redeploy.

diagnosis.summary: The storefront/frontend deployment was updated today to pull image nginx:1.299-alpine, which does not exist on docker.io (NotFound). The single pod is stuck in ImagePullBackOff, so the deployment has 0/1 ready replicas. Fix: point the Deployment at a valid image tag.

findings.name: thumbnailer
findings.root_cause: log-shipper sidecar buffers 4Mi files into emptyDir /buffer in a loop (upstream collector unreachable) and the container has a 20Mi ephemeral-storage limit; the pod exceeds it and is evicted, so the Deployment recreates pods every few minutes.
findings.fix: Raise or remove the log-shipper ephemeral-storage limit (and add sizeLimit to the buffer emptyDir), and restore the upstream log collector connection so logs are shipped instead of buffered indefinitely.

diagnosis.summary: thumbnailer pods in media are repeatedly evicted: the log-shipper sidecar writes 4Mi batches to an emptyDir /buffer while its upstream collector is unreachable, exceeding the 20Mi ephemeral-storage limit set on that container, so the kubelet evicts the pod and the Deployment replaces it. Root cause object: Deployment thumbnailer (log-shipper container spec). Two evicted pod instances observed with matching events."

findings.name: nightly-export
findings.root_cause: The nightly export job writes to /exports/orders-*.csv but its pod spec mounts no writable volume at that path (no PVC exists in the namespace), so both attempts fail with 'permission denied: cannot write', exit code 2, and the Job hits BackoffLimitExceeded — hence no export file was produced.
findings.fix: Add a writable volume (e.g. a PVC or emptyDir) mounted at /exports in the Job's pod template so the export can write its CSV; then re-run the job.

diagnosis.summary: The exports/nightly-export Job did not produce a file because it fails before writing: both pods exited 2 with 'permission denied: cannot write /exports/orders-2026-09-27.csv'. The pod spec has no volumes and no PVC exists in the namespace, so /exports is not writable storage. The Job hit BackoffLimitExceeded after 2 failures. Fix: mount a writable volume at /exports in the Job pod template.

findings.name: defaults
findings.root_cause: statement-builder sets no memory limit in its Deployment, so the namespace LimitRange 'defaults' injects a 32Mi default limit; the job loads ~50MB of ledger rows into memory, exceeds that injected limit and is OOMKilled (exit 137) on every start.
findings.fix: Set an explicit memory limit on the statement-builder container large enough for its working set (e.g. 128Mi), or raise/remove the 32Mi default in LimitRange 'defaults'.

diagnosis.summary: statement-builder crash-loops with OOMKilled (exit 137, 3 restarts). The Deployment declares no memory limits, but the finance namespace LimitRange 'defaults' injects a 32Mi default limit / 16Mi request; the workload's command buffers ~50MB, exceeding the injected limit. Root cause object to change: LimitRange 'defaults' (or add an explicit, adequate limit in the Deployment).

findings.name: report-worker
findings.root_cause: report-worker container is OOMKilled (exit 137) seconds after start because its memory limit of 32Mi is below what the workload needs; the kernel kill produces no application log, which is why the logs show no error.
findings.fix: raise the report-worker container memory limit (and request) above observed usage, e.g. to 128Mi/64Mi, or reduce in-process memory use

diagnosis.summary: report-worker in namespace reports crash-loops with no app-level error: the container is OOMKilled (reason OOMKilled, exit code 137, repeated restarts and BackOff events) because its 32Mi memory limit is too low for the workload. Fix is to raise the memory limit on the Deployment's container spec."

findings.name: checkout
findings.root_cause: Calls to the checkout service fail with connection refused because the Service selector (app: checkout-v2) does not match any pod; the Deployment labels its pods app: checkout, so the Service has 0 ready endpoints and traffic has nowhere to go.
findings.fix: Update the Service selector to app: checkout (or relabel the Deployment's pod template to app: checkout-v2) so the selector matches the running pods and endpoints populate.

diagnosis.summary: Checkout pods are healthy (1/1 ready, nginx running), but the checkout Service uses selector app: checkout-v2 while the Deployment labels pods app: checkout. The Service therefore has 0 matching pods and 0 ready endpoints, causing connection refused on all calls. Fix by aligning the Service selector with the pod labels.

findings.name: ledger
findings.root_cause: ledger container panics at startup with 'invalid config key "retries": expected integer, got "three"' and exits 2, so the pod crash-loops (3 restarts) and stays not ready
findings.fix: correct the ledger configuration value for 'retries' from the string 'three' to an integer (e.g. 3) in the deployment's config/env/ConfigMap

findings.name: ledger-api
findings.root_cause: Service ledger-api selects app=ledger-gateway but no pod carries that label (pods are labeled app=ledger and app=ledger-api), so it has 0 matching pods and 0 ready endpoints and never answers
findings.fix: point the service selector at the actual workload label (app=ledger-api) or add the app=ledger-gateway label to the ledger-api pods

diagnosis.summary: Two independent faults in namespace ledger: (1) Deployment 'ledger' crash-loops — its container panics on a bad config value ('retries' set to 'three' instead of an integer) and exits 2; (2) Service 'ledger-api' selects app=ledger-gateway which matches no pods (the running gateway pod is labeled app=ledger-api), leaving it with zero endpoints. The two symptoms in the report each have their own root cause."

findings.name: cache
findings.root_cause: cache pod is Pending/Unschedulable because the Deployment's nodeSelector requires disktype=nvme, but the only cluster node doctor-lab-control-plane is labeled disktype=standard, so 0/1 nodes match and no pod can ever run.
findings.fix: Remove or correct the nodeSelector (disktype: nvme) on the cache Deployment so it matches an existing node label (e.g. disktype=standard), or add an nvme-labeled node to the cluster.

diagnosis.summary: The cache deployment in namespace cache never gets a pod running: its pod carries nodeSelector disktype=nvme, while the sole node doctor-lab-control-plane has disktype=standard, so the scheduler reports 0/1 nodes available (FailedScheduling). The Deployment itself is otherwise trivial (busybox sleep, no resources); the fix is to change the node selector in the Deployment spec.

findings.name: pricing-api
findings.root_cause: Clients calling the pricing-api Service get connection refused because the Service forwards port 80 to targetPort 8080, but the pricing-api container (nginx) listens on containerPort 80 — so traffic hits a closed port even though the pod is healthy and ready.
findings.fix: Change the pricing-api Service targetPort from 8080 to 80 to match the container's listening port (or make the app listen on 8080).

diagnosis.summary: pricing-api pods are Running/Ready (container nginx listens on containerPort 80, readiness probe on :80 passes), but the pricing-api Service maps port 80 -> targetPort 8080, which nothing in the pod listens on. Traffic to the Service therefore gets connection refused while the pods look healthy. Fix: set the Service targetPort to 80.

findings.name: team-quota
findings.root_cause: renderer scaled to 5 but only 2 pods run because ResourceQuota team-quota caps the namespace at pods=2 (used: 2); every new pod creation is rejected with 'exceeded quota: team-quota, requested: pods=1, used: pods=2, limited: pods=2'.
findings.fix: Raise the pods limit in ResourceQuota batch/team-quota (hard.pods from 2 to at least 5) or move renderer to a namespace/quota with capacity.

diagnosis.summary: renderer Deployment in batch wants 5 replicas but only 2 exist. The ReplicaSet repeatedly fails to create pods with 'forbidden: exceeded quota: team-quota, requested: pods=1, used: pods=2, limited: pods=2' (FailedCreate events, deployment condition ReplicaFailure). ResourceQuota batch/team-quota confirms hard.pods=2, used.pods=2. Fix: raise the quota's pods limit; no workload fault.

findings.name: ml-trainer
findings.root_cause: ml-trainer's pod requests 64 CPU (a malformed unit — the scheduler treats it as 64 cores, not 64 millicores) on a node with only 2 allocatable cores, so the scheduler reports '1 Insufficient cpu' and preemption is not helpful, leaving the pod Pending.
findings.fix: Fix the ml-trainer container CPU request to a valid value that fits the cluster, e.g. change cpu: "64" to cpu: "64m" (or another value ≤ 2 cores).

diagnosis.summary: ml-trainer has been Pending because its single pod cannot be scheduled: the container's CPU request is written as \"64\" (interpreted as 64 cores), while the only node (doctor-lab-control-plane) has just 2 allocatable cores. The scheduler event confirms 'Insufficient cpu' and preemption being unhelpful. Fixing the request to a sane value (e.g. 64m) in the Deployment spec resolves it.

findings.name: web
findings.root_cause: Readiness probe HTTP GETs port 8081, but the nginx container listens on its default port 80 (no custom config or env set), so every probe gets 'connection refused' and the pod stays NotReady (0/1) with no traffic.
findings.fix: Point the readiness probe at port 80 (nginx's actual listen port), or configure nginx to listen on 8081 via a mounted config / NGINX_PORT env var.

diagnosis.summary: web Deployment is 0/1 ready: its readiness probe targets http://:8081/ but the stock nginx:1.29-alpine container listens on port 80 (logs show normal startup, no restarts, no custom config). Probe fails with connection refused (event x25), so the pod never becomes Ready and receives no traffic. Fix is in the Deployment spec: probe port 80 instead of 8081 (or make nginx listen on 8081). No Service exists in the namespace; the root cause is the probe/container port mismatch.

findings.name: search-web
findings.root_cause: The liveness probe runs a busy-loop (300k iterations) before its wget health check, so it always exceeds timeoutSeconds=1; kubelet kills the healthy container every few minutes, which looks like restarts with no errors in app logs.
findings.fix: Fix the search-web Deployment livenessProbe: remove the busy-loop from the exec command (just 'wget -q -O /dev/null http://127.0.0.1/') and/or raise timeoutSeconds above 1s.

diagnosis.summary: search-web pod is in CrashLoopBackOff not because the app crashes but because its liveness probe fails: the probe's exec script contains a 300,000-iteration busy loop before the actual HTTP check, guaranteeing it exceeds the 1s timeout. Kubelet kills the otherwise healthy nginx container (exit code 0/Completed), causing the observed restarts with clean logs. Fix belongs in the search-web Deployment's livenessProbe spec."

findings.name: catalog
findings.root_cause: Hotfix rollout set the catalog image to nginx:1.29-alpine-hotfix, which does not exist in docker.io/library (NotFound), so the new ReplicaSet's pod is stuck in ImagePullBackOff and the ProgressDeadlineExceeded leaves the old-version pods serving users.
findings.fix: Point the catalog Deployment at an image tag that actually exists in the registry (verify the hotfix was pushed, e.g. correct repository/tag or digest), then retrigger the rollout; roll back to the previous image if the hotfix must wait.

diagnosis.summary: The catalog hotfix deploy created ReplicaSet catalog-58664cc6f with image nginx:1.29-alpine-hotfix, but that tag does not resolve in docker.io/library (ErrImagePull NotFound), so its pod is in ImagePullBackOff and the deployment reports ProgressDeadlineExceeded. The two pre-hotfix replicas (catalog-86c9fdb8c6) remain Ready and are still serving the old version, which is why users see no change. Fix: use a valid image reference for the hotfix (or roll back).

findings.fix: Lower reporting-api requests to ~10m CPU / 8Mi (≈2× observed p95). Leave ingest-worker alone: it is pinned at its 50m CPU limit (throttled, may need more). Cache is already minimal.
findings.name: reporting-api
findings.root_cause: reporting-api requests 300m CPU and 256Mi memory but observed usage is ~0m CPU / 3Mi across the sample window, leaving ~$7.69/month of idle request cost — the largest waste in analytics.

diagnosis.summary: Rightsize audit of analytics: only reporting-api is materially over-provisioned (300m/256Mi requested vs ~0m/3Mi used, ~$7.69/mo idle); recommend 10m/8Mi. ingest-worker runs pinned at its 50m CPU limit (throttling risk, never cut) and cache's requests are already tiny (~$0.25/mo), so neither warrants a change. Note the sample window was short (10 samples), hence medium confidence on reporting-api.

diagnosis.summary: search-web restarts with no app errors because its liveness probe is broken: the exec probe runs a 300k-iteration busy loop before the HTTP check but timeoutSeconds is only 1, so it always times out. The container itself is healthy (last exit code 0); kubelet kills it after failureThreshold=2, causing CrashLoopBackOff. Root cause is the livenessProbe spec in Deployment search-web — remove the busy loop, use a plain wget/httpGet probe, and raise the timeout.
